name: Molybdenum cofactor deficiency
aliases: combined deficiency of sulphite oxidase, xanthine oxidase and aldehyde oxidase

reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive disorder of molybdenum cofactor biosynthesis, most commonly due to MOCS1 variants, with MOCS2 and GPHN also implicated
The molybdenum cofactor is required by sulphite oxidase, xanthine oxidase/dehydrogenase and aldehyde oxidase, so all three enzyme activities are lost together
Loss of sulphite oxidase activity drives the severe neurological phenotype through accumulation of neurotoxic sulphite
Presents in the neonatal period with intractable seizures, feeding difficulties, marked hypotonia progressing to spasticity and rapid encephalopathy, often mimicking hypoxic-ischaemic injury
Biochemical clues include raised urinary sulphite and S-sulphocysteine with low plasma uric acid and low urinary urate reflecting xanthine oxidase deficiency
Lens dislocation (ectopia lentis) develops over time, as in isolated sulphite oxidase deficiency
Type A disease (MOCS1) can respond to substrate replacement with cyclic pyranopterin monophosphate if started very early
It is clinically and biochemically indistinguishable from isolated sulphite oxidase deficiency except for the low uric acid
reference.pathophysiology: Molybdenum cofactor is a pterin-based cofactor synthesised through a multistep pathway (involving MOCS1, MOCS2 and gephyrin) that is essential for the activity of the molybdoenzymes sulphite oxidase, xanthine oxidase/dehydrogenase and aldehyde oxidase. When cofactor synthesis fails, all three enzymes are inactive. The most damaging consequence is loss of sulphite oxidase, which normally converts sulphite to sulphate in cysteine catabolism; sulphite accumulates and is directly neurotoxic, while S-sulphocysteine builds up and may act as an excitotoxin. Xanthine oxidase deficiency additionally causes low uric acid and elevated hypoxanthine and xanthine. The combined effect is severe, progressive neonatal brain injury with cystic encephalomalacia.
additionalDifferentials: Neonatal epileptic encephalopathies of other causes
Neonatal-onset organic acidaemias or urea cycle disorders
additionalInvestigations: Fresh urine sulphite testing (dipstick) and quantitation of urinary S-sulphocysteine
Plasma uric acid, which is characteristically low (distinguishing it from isolated sulphite oxidase deficiency)
Plasma total homocysteine, which tends to be low
Neuroimaging showing diffuse injury, cystic change and later cerebral atrophy
Molecular genetic testing of MOCS1, MOCS2 and GPHN
redFlags: Intractable neonatal seizures with rapidly progressive encephalopathy
Imaging suggesting hypoxic-ischaemic injury without a supporting perinatal history
Low plasma uric acid in an encephalopathic neonate
reference.prognosis: The classic neonatal form is usually devastating, with profound neurodevelopmental impairment and early death. Type A (MOCS1) disease may respond to early substrate replacement therapy, so prognosis can improve markedly when treatment is started before irreversible brain injury; type B and other genetic forms currently lack specific treatment.
pitfalls: Mistaking the presentation for hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy and not testing for the metabolic cause
Missing the treatable MOCS1 form by delaying genetic and biochemical diagnosis
Relying on delayed urine sulphite testing, as sulphite degrades rapidly in stored samples
Failing to distinguish it from isolated sulphite oxidase deficiency by checking uric acid
references: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease
management: For type A (MOCS1) disease, substrate replacement with cyclic pyranopterin monophosphate (fosdenopterin) is disease-specific and should be started as early as possible, ideally before irreversible brain injury
Type B and other genetic subtypes have no available substrate therapy and are managed supportively
Dietary reduction of sulphur-containing amino acids as an adjunct to limit accumulation of neurotoxic sulphite and S-sulphocysteine
Seizure control with antiepileptic drugs, and management of feeding difficulty with nasogastric or gastrostomy feeding alongside management of hypotonia and spasticity
Biochemical monitoring of urinary sulphite and S-sulphocysteine, plasma urate and homocysteine to track treatment response, with ophthalmological review for ectopia lentis
Multidisciplinary input from metabolic medicine, neurology, dietetics and, where the phenotype is severe, palliative care
Genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance, with family screening and prenatal diagnosis
